labels.equivalent: no reachable input makes observable behaviour differ (strict)
labels.junk: equivalent, or mutates something no reasonable test would assert on
labels.source: hand labels from BENCHMARKS.md Runs B and D; every survivor re-read by hand

survivors.description: A cache created with capacity=0 is accepted instead of rejected, so callers get a cache that silently can never store anything.
The default cache capacity is smaller than documented (100 instead of 128), so callers relying on the default silently get less caching headroom and see extra evictions.
survivors.note: Changes a default nobody pins with a test (capacity 128 -> 100).

survivors.description: len(cache) undercounts by one, so callers relying on the reported size see one fewer entry than actually stored.
len(cache) always reports zero regardless of how many entries are stored, breaking any capacity or emptiness check based on it.
len(cache) overcounts by one, so callers relying on the reported size see one more entry than actually stored.
Reading a key from the cache no longer marks it as recently used, so it can be evicted even though it was just accessed.
A cache hit is recorded as a miss, so hit/miss statistics used for monitoring cache effectiveness are wrong.
The cache evicts one entry too early, dropping the least-recently-used item before the cache is actually full.
Overwriting an existing key's value does not refresh its recency, so it can be evicted as if it hadn't been touched recently.

Invalidating a key that was never cached returns None instead of False, so callers checking the boolean result of invalidate() get an unexpected falsy-but-wrong value that can break stricter checks like `is False`.
survivors.note: Returns None instead of False for an absent key; violates the contract but only an `is False` check distinguishes it. Counted as junk, conservative.

survivors.description: invalidate_prefix reports how many keys it removed but never actually deletes them, so cached values keep being served after they should have been invalidated.
invalidate_prefix matches keys by suffix instead of prefix, so it silently fails to invalidate the keys callers actually meant to clear and may clear unrelated ones.
invalidate_prefix under-reports the number of keys removed by one, which throws off any caller (or logging/metrics) that relies on the count to confirm the right number of entries were cleared.
has_next stays true on the last page, so pagers try to fetch a page beyond the end of the data.
has_next is backwards: it reports no next page while more pages remain, and reports a next page once you're past the end.
has_next computes the page count with the arguments swapped, producing a wildly wrong result whenever total and per_page differ, so pagination stops or continues at the wrong point.
has_prev reports true even on the first page, so pagers show a 'previous' control that leads nowhere.
has_prev stays false on page 2 as well as page 1, so users can't navigate back to the second page.
has_prev is inverted and is essentially always false, so the previous-page control never appears even when earlier pages exist.
page_count silently drops the ceiling: 11 items at 5 per page reports 2 pages instead of 3, so the last partial page of results is missed entirely.
page_count rejects a valid per_page of exactly 1, so callers who page one item at a time get an unexpected ValueError.
Calling paginate() with items=None crashes instead of being treated as an empty result set.
paginate() accepts per_page=0, silently returning an empty page forever instead of rejecting the invalid input.

The page's reported total item count is the size of the current slice instead of the whole collection, so has_next/has_prev and downstream page counts silently become wrong once results span more than one page.
Durations with surrounding whitespace like ' 1h30m ' are rejected instead of parsed, because the input is no longer trimmed before parsing.
A duration with a trailing number and no unit, like '1h30', silently drops the trailing amount instead of raising, so the parsed duration is smaller than what the caller wrote.
A value that itself contains an '=' character, like 'a=b=c', crashes instead of splitting on only the first '=' as documented.
Leading and trailing whitespace around values is preserved instead of stripped, so ' a = 1 ' keeps stray spaces in the parsed value.
When the same key appears twice, the first value silently wins instead of the later one overriding it as documented.
A max_discount cap acts as a minimum instead of a maximum, so discounts meant to be capped can end up larger than intended.
Passing percent=None, which is documented as 'no discount', instead applies a full 100% discount, making the item free.
The discounted price is rounded to one decimal place instead of two cents of precision, silently losing sub-cent accuracy that downstream billing code expects.
Text exactly as long as the limit gets truncated and suffixed anyway instead of being returned unchanged.
When the limit is smaller than the suffix itself, truncate returns the full suffix instead of trimming it to fit, so the result can exceed the requested limit.
Truncated text is cut one character shorter than necessary before the suffix is appended, silently discarding an extra character of content that would have fit within the limit.

The default capacity boundary check allows capacity of 0 to silently pass validation logic when capacity is set below 1 via a boundary flip, causing an off-by-one on the minimum allowed capacity so capacity=1 is wrongly rejected.
Hit and miss counters start at 1 instead of 0, so freshly created caches report inflated hit/miss statistics before any access occurs.
The default capacity is silently changed from 128 to 1, so caches created without an explicit capacity evict everything after the very first insert.
survivors.note: Default capacity 128 -> 1; changes a default nobody pins (Run B precedent).

survivors.description: len(cache) always returns one less than the actual number of entries stored
len(cache) always returns zero regardless of how many items are stored
Reading a value from the cache no longer refreshes its recency, so recently-accessed items can still be evicted before less-recently-used ones.
Every cache lookup, hit or miss, is counted as a hit, so hit/miss statistics become meaningless.
Setting a value for a key that already exists no longer refreshes its recency, so it can be evicted as if it were the oldest entry even though it was just updated.
invalidate() reports success even when the key was never present, since it always returns True regardless of whether a deletion happened
invalidate() removes the key from storage but leaves it in the LRU order tracking, so stale key references can linger and affect eviction ordering
survivors.note: del d[key] -> d.pop(key): binary-identical on an OrderedDict.

survivors.description: invalidate_prefix always reports zero removals regardless of how many keys were actually deleted, so callers relying on the count get wrong information
invalidate_prefix silently does nothing (removes no keys) but still reports a truthy-looking count based on matches found before deletion is skipped
invalidate_prefix only removes keys that exactly match the prefix elsewhere in the string rather than keys starting with it, so prefix-based invalidation of nested namespaces silently fails
has_next incorrectly reports True on the last page because it treats the current page as still having more pages until it exceeds the count by one
has_next always returns False, so callers never see a next-page indicator even when more pages exist
has_next is inverted, reporting no next page when one exists and vice versa
On the first page, has_prev incorrectly reports True instead of False, suggesting there is a previous page when there isn't.
has_prev always returns False, so the UI never shows a 'previous page' link even when one exists.
has_prev is inverted, returning True only on the first page and False everywhere else.
page_count silently returns 0 for negative totals instead of treating them as invalid, masking upstream bugs that pass a negative count.
survivors.note: total <= 0 -> total < 0: observable only for negative totals, a degenerate input.

survivors.description: Calling page_count with per_page exactly 1 now incorrectly raises a ValueError even though 1 is a valid page size.
The 'total' count reported on a page is always one less than the true number of items, making has_next and other calculations based on total slightly wrong.
Duration strings with a trailing number but no unit (e.g. '1h30') silently succeed instead of raising an error, returning only the hours portion

Whitespace-only input like a string of spaces is treated as empty before stripping is checked, but leading/trailing whitespace inside mixed durations like '1h 30m' now silently drops the space instead of raising, changing which strings are accepted vs rejected inconsistently
Passing an empty string after stripping (e.g. all-whitespace input) no longer raises immediately and instead falls through, eventually raising a different, less specific error about no duration found
survivors.note: Both variants raise ValueError on empty input; only the message text differs.

survivors.description: Values are no longer stripped of surrounding whitespace, so keys like 'a' end up mapped to ' 1' instead of '1'.
An empty input string now returns None instead of an empty dict, breaking any caller that iterates or does membership checks on the result.
When the same key appears multiple times, the first occurrence wins instead of the last, contradicting the documented override behavior.

The discount cap is ignored when the computed discount is smaller than max_discount, effectively swapping which value is used as the cap versus the actual discount, so discounts can exceed the intended maximum in some cases.
Negative percent values are silently accepted instead of raising an error, since the boundary check no longer rejects them.
Passing percent=None now raises an error instead of being treated as no discount, breaking callers that rely on this documented fallback behavior.
A capacity of 0 is accepted instead of rejected, creating a cache that can never usefully hold anything.
Hit counter starts at one instead of zero, so hit statistics are always inflated.
len(cache) reports one fewer item than the cache actually holds.
len(cache) always reports zero regardless of how many entries are stored.
Reading a key no longer refreshes its recency, so recently-read entries are evicted first.
A cache miss is counted as a hit, corrupting hit/miss statistics.
Successful lookups are not counted as hits, so the hit counter stays at zero.
Overwriting an existing key does not mark it as recently used, so a freshly updated entry can be evicted before older ones.
The cache evicts an entry as soon as it reaches capacity, so it only ever holds capacity-1 items.
Invalidating a key that isn't in the cache reports success instead of failure.
Invalidating by prefix reports one fewer key removed than it actually dropped.
Invalidating by prefix leaves the first matching key in the cache, so stale values keep being served.
Invalidating by prefix also drops keys that merely contain the prefix anywhere, wiping unrelated entries.
has_next stays true on the final page, so callers keep requesting a page that does not exist.
has_next is computed from the item count instead of the page count, so it is true for almost every page.
has_next reports whether there is a previous page instead of a next one.
The first page incorrectly reports that a previous page exists.
Pages after the first report that no previous page exists, and page 1 falsely reports one.
Page 2 incorrectly reports that there is no previous page.
Partial final pages are dropped, so a partly-filled last page of items becomes unreachable (11 items at 5 per page reports 2 pages instead of 3).
A per_page of 1 is rejected as invalid instead of being accepted.
Pages after the first start one item too early, so each page repeats the last item of the previous page.
The reported total counts only the items on the current page instead of the whole collection, so page counts and has_next are wrong.
Requesting per_page=0 is silently accepted and returns an empty page instead of raising an error.
Whitespace is no longer stripped from the input, so durations with surrounding spaces are rejected as invalid characters.
A trailing number without a unit is silently ignored instead of raising an error, so "1h30" parses as one hour.
Empty input returns zero instead of raising a ValueError.
Earlier occurrences of a duplicate key win instead of the last one overriding.
Values keep their surrounding whitespace instead of being stripped.
survivors.note: Adds a redundant value.strip('\n'); the value is fully stripped two lines later.

survivors.description: The discount cap is ignored and instead the larger of the computed discount and the cap is applied, so capped discounts overcharge the customer's savings.
A percent of None is treated as a full 100% discount instead of no discount.
A percent of exactly 100 is rejected as out of range instead of applying a full discount.
Falsy values other than None (like empty strings or 0) are turned into empty strings instead of being normalized normally.
